subChunks.title: Layered Architecture, Coupling & Cohesion
subChunks.hookHtml: Individual methods and classes are the bricks. Architecture is how you arrange them into a building. Without intentional architecture, every system eventually becomes a ball of mud — where every class knows about every other class, and changing anything risks breaking everything.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Layered Architecture

The most common architecture pattern in Java applications: organise code into horizontal layers, each with a single responsibility.

┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│     Controller (Presentation)       │  ← HTTP concerns
│  Handles HTTP requests, responses   │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│     Service (Business Logic)        │  ← Application rules
│  Orchestrates business operations   │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│     Repository (Data Access)        │  ← Persistence concerns
│  Reads and writes to the database   │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│     Domain (Model)                  │  ← Core entities
│  Spell, Mage, Enrolment, etc.       │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

Dependency rule: each layer only calls the layer below it. Controllers call Services. Services call Repositories. Nothing calls upward. Domain classes have no dependencies on any other layer.

Separation of Concerns

Each class has one reason to change. A SpellService contains business logic — spell validation, XP calculation, eligibility rules. It does not parse HTTP, format JSON, or write SQL. When the database changes, only the Repository changes. When the API changes, only the Controller changes.

Coupling

Coupling measures how much a class knows about or depends on another. High coupling = changing one class requires changing many others. Low coupling = classes are independent and can be changed, replaced, or tested in isolation.

Common coupling reducers: interfaces (depend on an abstraction, not a concrete implementation), dependency injection (receive your dependencies; don't create them), event-driven communication.

Cohesion

Cohesion measures how related a class's responsibilities are. High cohesion = the class does one thing well. Low cohesion = the class contains unrelated responsibilities.

A class that handles HTTP parsing AND business logic AND database queries is low-cohesion. Split it: one class per responsibility.

The Dependency Inversion Principle

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions (interfaces). This is the 'D' in SOLID:

// BAD — Service depends directly on concrete class
class SpellService {
    private MySQLSpellRepository repo = new MySQLSpellRepository();
}

// GOOD — Service depends on an interface
class SpellService {
    private final SpellRepository repo;  // interface
    SpellService(SpellRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; } // DI
}

storyBeats.text: The Academy's oldest tower was built without a plan. Walls were added as needed; staircases were retrofitted through existing rooms; the heating system runs through the library. Forty years later, nobody dares touch the fourth floor because nobody knows what will collapse. The new tower has blueprints.

storyBeats.speaker: Chief Architect Sorel
storyBeats.text: Software architecture is how you prevent your system from becoming the old tower. Layered architecture is the simplest pattern that works for most Java applications: Controllers for HTTP, Services for business logic, Repositories for data. Each layer knows only about the layer directly below it.

storyBeats.speaker: Layered architecture in a Spring Boot app
Chief Architect Sorel
storyBeats.text: Coupling and cohesion are the two metrics of structural quality. High coupling means your classes are entangled — difficult to change or test in isolation. High cohesion means each class does exactly one thing — easy to understand, test, and replace. Aim for low coupling and high cohesion.

storyBeats.speaker: Chief Architect Sorel
storyBeats.text: The Dependency Inversion Principle says: depend on interfaces, not concrete classes. Your SpellService should not know whether the data comes from MySQL, Postgres, or a test mock — it should only know that it can call save() and findById(). Spring's dependency injection wires the concrete implementation in for you.

learningObjectives: Describe the three layers of a typical layered architecture and the responsibility of each
Explain the dependency rule: which direction dependencies flow between layers
Define coupling and cohesion and explain the goal (low coupling, high cohesion)
Apply the Dependency Inversion Principle by injecting an interface rather than instantiating a concrete class
commonMistakes: Calling a Controller from a Service or a Repository from a Controller — violates the dependency rule
Putting business logic in the Controller — couples HTTP concerns with application rules
Creating concrete dependencies inside a class instead of injecting them — prevents testing and replacement
Making every method in a class public 'just in case' — exposes internals and increases coupling
assessmentCriteria: Can draw or describe a three-layer architecture and assign each class to the correct layer
Can identify a layered architecture violation (e.g. business logic in a Controller) and explain why it's a problem
Can refactor a constructor that instantiates its own dependencies to accept them via injection
Can explain what would have to change at each layer if the database was switched from MySQL to MongoDB
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain layered architecture to a junior developer who puts all their code in the main class. What are the layers? Why do they exist? What does 'separation of concerns' actually prevent?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Given this class, answer the following:

public class SpellHandler {
    public void handleRequest(String spellId, HttpRequest req) {
        // Parse HTTP body
        String json = req.getBody();
        Spell spell = parseJson(json);
        // Business rule
        if (spell.getDamage() > 500) spell.setDamage(500); 
        // Database write
        Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:mysql://...");
        PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("UPDATE spells...");
        ps.executeUpdate();
        // Format HTTP response
        respond(200, toJson(spell));
    }
}
  1. Name every layered architecture concern this class violates
  2. Describe how you would split this into three classes following the layered pattern
  3. If you needed to swap MySQL for PostgreSQL, how many classes would need to change in your refactored version? Why?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Violations:
   - HTTP parsing AND response formatting belong in a Controller layer
   - Business rule (damage cap) belongs in a Service layer
   - Database connection and SQL belongs in a Repository layer
   - SpellHandler does ALL of these — zero separation of concerns, maximum coupling

2. Split into three classes:
   SpellController: handles HttpRequest parsing and response formatting; calls SpellService
   SpellService: applies the damage cap rule; calls SpellRepository
   SpellRepository: handles DB connection and PreparedStatement; returns Spell

3. In the refactored version: only SpellRepository needs to change when switching databases.
   SpellService depends on a SpellRepository interface — it doesn't care whether the implementation is MySQL or PostgreSQL. SpellController depends on SpellService — equally unaffected.
   One class to change instead of touching everything.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Design the layered architecture for a simple Order Management System. The system accepts HTTP requests to place orders, calculates the total price including discounts (10% for Gold members), saves orders to a database, and sends a confirmation email.

Write: (a) the three (or four) classes/interfaces you would create, (b) the layer each belongs to, (c) what each class's single responsibility is, (d) the email sending — which layer does it belong to, and how would you inject the email service to keep the OrderService testable?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a)+(b) Classes and layers:
  OrderController (Presentation) — handles HTTP POST /orders, parses request body, returns 201 response
  OrderService (Business Logic) — validates order, calculates total with discount rules, calls OrderRepository and EmailService
  OrderRepository (Data Access) — implements OrderRepository interface; saves order to DB
  EmailService (interface) + EmailServiceImpl (Infrastructure) — sends confirmation email

(c) Single responsibilities:
  OrderController: HTTP translation only — maps request to domain objects, maps result to HTTP response
  OrderService: all business logic — discount calculation, validation, coordination
  OrderRepository: persistence only — SQL or JPA, no business logic
  EmailService: send an email with order details

(d) Email service:
  Email is infrastructure — belongs in its own layer (infrastructure/external), injected into OrderService:
  class OrderService {
      OrderService(OrderRepository repo, EmailService emailer) {...}
      // emailer is an interface — in tests, inject a mock; in production, inject SMTP impl
  }
  This keeps OrderService testable without a real SMTP server — pass a mock EmailService in unit tests.

questions.prompt: In a layered architecture, which layer is responsible for business rules and application logic?
questions.explanation: The Service layer contains business logic — validation, calculations, orchestration of multiple repositories, and application-specific rules. The Controller handles HTTP. The Repository handles persistence. The Domain contains pure data structures (entities/value objects).

questions.prompt: In a properly layered application, it is acceptable for a Repository to call a Service to apply business rules before saving data.
questions.explanation: The dependency rule states that dependencies flow downward: Controller → Service → Repository. A Repository calling a Service would be a circular dependency that violates this rule. Business rules should be applied in the Service layer before the Repository is called.

questions.prompt: A UserService directly instantiates new MySQLUserRepository() inside its constructor. What problem does this cause?
options: It causes a NullPointerException at startup
It makes UserService impossible to unit test in isolation — you cannot inject a mock repository
Java does not allow instantiation inside a constructor
It increases cohesion at the expense of coupling
questions.answer: It makes UserService impossible to unit test in isolation — you cannot inject a mock repository
questions.explanation: When a class creates its own dependencies, you cannot substitute a test double. Unit tests of UserService would require a real database. Inject the interface: UserService(UserRepository repo) — then tests can pass new MockUserRepository(), production code passes the real one via Spring DI.
